documentation_gaps.title: Decision enforcement for invoice approvals is not documented
documentation_gaps.description: The documentation describes that the Invoice Agent reads an uploaded invoice JSON file, applies deny and approve rules via an LLM, and returns an approve or deny decision with reasoning, including a follow-up message that asks the agent to reconsider denied invoices as urgent, but it does not state what component ultimately enforces the decision or whether any deterministic layer re-applies the hard deny conditions independently of the model. As a result, it is unclear whether invoices that meet deny criteria (e.g., amount over $20,000 or unapproved category/submitter) can still be approved because of the model’s discretionary reasoning and conversational context, or whether another component or human review step ensures consistency with the documented deny policy before an invoice is treated as approved.
documentation_gaps.importance: Clarifying how the model’s approve/deny output is consumed and whether hard deny rules are re-enforced outside the LLM is necessary to determine if policy-inconsistent approvals described in the threat are actually possible in the deployed system.
requested_evidence: Architecture or workflow documentation describing which component consumes the model’s approve/deny decision and what it does with that output (e.g., whether it is treated as authoritative for payment).

Documentation or specification of any deterministic rule engine, validation layer, or post-processing that re-applies the deny conditions (amount over $20,000, unapproved category, unapproved submitter) after the LLM responds, before an invoice is considered approved.
Documentation of any human review or approval step for invoices that meet deny conditions but are nevertheless approved by the model, including criteria for when human intervention is required.

catalog_gap_candidates.concern: The invoice-approval workflow relies on an LLM’s discretionary reasoning over conversational context, including a system-authored urgent follow-up, to decide between hard deny rules and an approval rule, and there is no documented deterministic enforcement layer that guarantees the hard deny conditions are respected. This allows policy-inconsistent approvals where invoices that meet deny criteria can be effectively approved based on model discretion, weakening the integrity and predictability of business-rule enforcement.

nearest_requirements.why_not: req-AI-001 addresses treating untrusted source content as data and preventing instructions embedded in that untrusted content from altering the model’s task. In this threat, the problematic instructions (e.g., the urgent follow-up and direction to use "best discretion") are system-authored, and the risk arises from how the LLM is used as a discretionary decision-maker over conflicting rules, not from embedded instructions in untrusted input content.

req-AI-002 concerns validation of model output before external publication, focusing on structural and content checks for what is exposed outside the system. The threat here is about internal use of the model’s approve/deny decision as an authoritative control without a deterministic check against the documented deny rules, not about validating externally published content.
